title: Factual infographic: Cut Vinyl Decal Build and Apply
tests: Explains real cut-vinyl decal layers, transfer tape, weeding, registration, surface prep, squeegee pressure, and peel angle without fictional data.
prompt: Create a detailed factual infographic about real-world vinyl sign/decal construction and application, landscape 3:2 educational poster style, clean professional print-shop visual design. Subject: how a cut vinyl decal is built and applied. Include a large accurate exploded cross-section showing, from top to bottom: transfer tape, cut vinyl film, pressure-sensitive adhesive, cleaned substrate panel. Include a small squeegee-angle diagram showing firm overlapping strokes from center outward. Include a simple workflow strip: clean surface, hinge/tape position, peel liner, squeegee apply, remove transfer tape, post-check edges. Include close-up details: air-release path, edge seal/edge lift warning, substrate examples such as painted aluminum, acrylic, glass. Use clear factual labels with only short words: TRANSFER TAPE, VINYL FILM, ADHESIVE, SUBSTRATE, CLEAN, HINGE, PEEL, SQUEEGEE, REMOVE, CHECK EDGES. Avoid fake exact numbers, invented brands, logos, marketing slogans, fantasy, fictional elements, or decorative clutter. Use crisp vector-like diagrams mixed with realistic material textures, high contrast, readable hierarchy, technical but attractive, print-shop colors of white, graphite, cyan, red-orange, and brushed aluminum.

factualInfographic.topic: Cut vinyl decal construction and application
factualInfographic.description: A real-world sign-shop infographic showing how cut vinyl, adhesive, liner, transfer tape, weeding, alignment, surface prep, pressure, and peel angle fit together.

title: Factual infographic: Planted Aquarium Nitrogen Cycle
tests: Explains the real planted-aquarium nitrogen cycle, bacterial conversion, plant uptake, testing, water changes, oxygen, and overfeeding risk without fictional claims.
prompt: Create a detailed factual infographic about the real-world nitrogen cycle in a planted freshwater aquarium, landscape educational poster style, clean modern science illustration. Show a cross-section aquarium scene with substrate, rooted aquatic plants, filter, fish, and water column. Use accurate conservative relationships, no fake exact numbers. Include a clear cycle diagram: fish waste and uneaten food produce AMMONIA, beneficial bacteria convert AMMONIA to NITRITE, other beneficial bacteria convert NITRITE to NITRATE, plants use NITRATE and AMMONIUM for growth, water changes remove excess NITRATE, filter media provides bacterial surface area. Include a small root-zone panel showing roots taking up nutrients from substrate/water. Include a simple warning panel: TEST WATER, AVOID OVERFEEDING, ADD PLANTS SLOWLY. Labels should be short and readable: AMMONIA, NITRITE, NITRATE, BENEFICIAL BACTERIA, PLANT UPTAKE, FILTER MEDIA, WATER CHANGE, ROOT ZONE. No fantasy, no fictional species, no fake exact ppm values, no brand names, no logos, no invented data. Visual style: crisp scientific diagram mixed with realistic aquarium textures, lush green plants, clear blue water, clean arrows, high readability, tasteful color palette of deep green, cyan, white, charcoal, and small amber highlights.

factualInfographic.description: A real-world aquarium-care infographic showing how waste becomes ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate, how nitrifying bacteria and plants interact, and why testing and water changes matter.
factualInfographic.sourceNote: Real-world/non-fiction topic; conservative aquarium-care basics, no invented statistics.

title: Factual infographic: How a Thermal Receipt Fades
tests: Real-world non-fiction factual infographic; explains direct thermal receipt paper chemistry and fading factors; visually rich workbench infographic; no private data or fake statistics.
prompt:
Create a finished, highly detailed square factual infographic titled "How a Thermal Receipt Fades" explaining direct thermal receipt paper. Make it visually rich and accurate, like a museum-quality materials-science panel photographed on a tidy sign-shop/retail counter workbench, not a plain poster. Include concise readable labels only where useful. Show a layered paper cross-section with base paper, thermal coating with colorless dye and developer, protective/top coat, and a darkened printed area; a thermal print head pressing against paper with heat pixels activating the coating; a before/during/after strip showing fresh print, fading, and uneven brown-gray discoloration; and practical cause/storage panels covering heat, sunlight/UV, abrasion, hand oils, plasticizers from some plastics, solvents/cleaners, humidity, cool dry dark storage, keeping receipts away from vinyl/plastic sleeves and chemicals, and scanning or photographing important receipts. Add material swatches, a loupe, an unbranded heat gun set aside, a roll of thermal paper, generic receipt marks with no private data, tweezers, and a matte cutting-mat edge. Avoid brand logos, private data, fake exact statistics, invented chemistry, watermark, signature, copyrighted characters, dancing, and generic stock-photo styling.

Source photo needed: none.

Reusable fill-in-the-blank template: Create a finished square factual infographic titled [INFOGRAPHIC TITLE] explaining [REAL-WORLD MATERIAL, PROCESS, TOOL, OR OBJECT]. Make it visually rich and accurate, like a museum-quality [FIELD OR WORKSHOP] panel photographed on a believable [WORKBENCH OR ENVIRONMENT], not a plain poster. Include [CROSS-SECTION OR ANATOMY VIEW], [PROCESS DIAGRAM], [BEFORE/DURING/AFTER OR CAUSE/EFFECT SEQUENCE], [COMMON FAILURE MODES OR ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS], and [PRACTICAL CARE OR USE GUIDANCE]. Add tactile supporting objects such as [TOOLS], [SAMPLES], and [SURFACE DETAILS]. Use concise labels, conservative factual claims, and avoid fake exact statistics, brand logos, private data, and invented mechanisms.

What to preserve: real-world non-fiction accuracy, clear cause-and-effect explanation, material-layer detail, concise readable labels, tactile workshop context, and practical storage/use guidance.

What to change: adapt the topic, field, diagrams, failure modes, care guidance, sample objects, surrounding workbench, and visual palette while keeping the image factual and information-dense.

Example substitution: [INFOGRAPHIC TITLE] = How a Thermal Receipt Fades; [REAL-WORLD MATERIAL, PROCESS, TOOL, OR OBJECT] = direct thermal receipt paper; [FIELD OR WORKSHOP] = materials-science/sign-shop; [WORKBENCH OR ENVIRONMENT] = tidy retail counter workbench; [CROSS-SECTION OR ANATOMY VIEW] = layered receipt paper coating; [PROCESS DIAGRAM] = thermal print head heat pixels activating dye/developer chemistry; [BEFORE/DURING/AFTER OR CAUSE/EFFECT SEQUENCE] = fresh, fading, and aged/discolored receipt samples; [COMMON FAILURE MODES OR ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS] = heat, sunlight/UV, abrasion, oils, plasticizers, solvents, humidity, and poor storage; [PRACTICAL CARE OR USE GUIDANCE] = keep cool, dry, dark, away from some plastics/chemicals, and scan important receipts; [TOOLS] = loupe, tweezers, thermal paper roll, unbranded heat gun, and material swatches.

factualInfographic.description: A real-world materials-science infographic explaining how direct thermal receipt paper forms marks through heat-activated coating chemistry and why heat, UV, abrasion, oils, plasticizers, solvents, humidity, and poor storage can fade it.
